text: I'm Jinlan Zhao. **What the Fingers Hear connects a physical Braille music score with audio playback.** Readers select a measure by touch and request the parts they want to hear. Today I'll show the new controls and voice interaction, the research plan, and the next features for musicians.

comments.text: Hi everyone. I'm Jinlan Zhao, and I study Electronic Production and Design at Berklee. My project, What the Fingers Hear, explores audio navigation from a physical Braille music score. A reader selects a measure with their finger and uses an explicit command to hear the music. I'm interested in how music technology can support that connection between touch and listening. In my last report, the camera and gesture playback path worked, while voice-selected instruments were still planned. Today I'll focus on the physical controls and voice interaction I have added since then, the changes that helped, and what I still need to test.

comments.text: The last demonstration raised a problem with repeated or unclear gesture activation. I added physical buttons as another input method to test. RECORD works as push-to-talk. I hold it while speaking, and releasing it submits the request. PLAY starts the Full Mix from the selected measure. STOP stops playback and cancels recording or a pending request. The controls use a Teensy board with debounced button events. These buttons give me a more explicit control path for development. I still need to compare them with gestures before deciding which method works better for Braille music readers.

text: Direct PLAY and gestures can send playback commands without speech recognition.

OpenCV and ArUco establish page coordinates. MediaPipe tracks the fingertip, and the page map identifies the measure. **Starting RECORD freezes that measure for the request.** Local Whisper transcribes speech, Qwen2.5:7b interprets it, and Python validates the command before sending OSC to Max/MSP. Max handles playback and synchronization. Direct PLAY and gestures send transport commands directly.

comments.text: The prototype now connects position selection, speech and playback. OpenCV and ArUco establish page coordinates, while MediaPipe estimates the fingertip position. A prepared page map converts that position into a measure number. When RECORD begins, the controller freezes the selected measure for that request. Local Whisper transcribes the speech, and a local Qwen model interprets it. Python checks the command before sending OSC to Max. Max handles the audio and synchronization. Direct PLAY and gestures can bypass speech recognition. The current setup runs on my Mac, and the spoken responses use macOS speech output. I haven't validated portability or measured end-to-end latency yet.

**Voice requests select a single instrument, several instruments, or a measure range.** “Play violin one” uses the captured measure. “Play flute one and cello from measure eight to twelve” sets both parts and range. If I say “Play flute,” the system asks “Flute one, flute two, or both?” **The answer keeps the original measure, even if my finger moves.** Selected stems share a signal-rate playhead, while Full Mix uses a stereo player. The prepared piece contains sixteen measures.

comments.text: Voice-selected playback was still future work in the previous report. It now supports a single instrument, several instruments, and an explicit measure range. For example, play violin one uses the measure captured when recording begins. Play flute one and cello from measure eight to twelve specifies both the instruments and the range. The screenshot shows Max receiving single-stem and multistem commands during development. Full Mix still uses its separate stereo player. Selected stems share a signal-rate playhead, which keeps them aligned. This currently works with the prepared sixteen-measure piece and its registered page map.

The regex parser struggled with natural wording. **The current parser uses ordered decision steps and 34 examples, with Python handling corrections and exclusions.** Local Ollama inference replaced the API after rate limits interrupted development. Regex remains the fallback. **The October 12 report records 31 transcript-based parser cases passing.** The next fixes address “full mix” becoming “four mix” in transcription and terminal messages that disagree with corrected tracks.

comments.text: The first voice parser used regular expressions. It handled fixed phrases, but it struggled with natural variation and corrections. I then tried a language model. A rules-only prompt still produced missing fields and unnecessary clarification. The current prompt uses ordered decision steps and thirty-four examples. I also found that the model did not reliably remove an earlier instrument after a self-correction, so Python now handles corrections and exclusions. I moved from the planned API path to local Ollama inference after hitting development rate limits. The deterministic parser remains an error fallback. These changes helped the recorded development cases, but they still need broader testing.

text: **I am completing CITI training and preparing the IRB application**, including the protocol and consent materials. I plan three studies: **usability** through touch and voice tasks, **buttons versus gestures** on equivalent transport tasks, and **interaction rules and customization**. I will collect success, errors, recovery behavior and participant feedback. Studies 2 and 3 compare conditions within participants, with counterbalanced order and comparable practice and feedback. Recruitment and data collection will follow written approval. **While IRB review takes time, I will develop the next interactions.**

comments.text: I drafted a protocol with three related studies. The first examines usability through touch and voice tasks. The second compares buttons and gestures for equivalent Play and Stop operations. The third examines fixed interaction defaults and user customization. The controlled comparisons are planned within participants, with counterbalanced order. I want to collect task outcomes, errors, interruptions, recovery behavior and participant feedback. I will only compare autonomous system performance when both conditions are implemented and checked. Proposed behaviors shown through a script will be labeled and analyzed separately. These studies are planned, and participant data collection has not started.

name: data-source

**A rest, a failed request and an unknown position each need different feedback.** For example: “Flute one rests here. Its next entry is measure eight. Would you like the two measures before it enters?” **MusicXML supplies rests, active instruments and the next entry.** Command and tracking status explain system errors. This lets a reader ask which instruments play here, hear the lead-in or choose another part.

name: context
text: Planned interaction · Keep the same measure range

name: purpose
text: Compare shared rhythms, musical responses and the melody in context.

**Keep the same range while changing the listening combination:** “Play my part,” “Add cello,” “Play the Full Mix,” and “Restore the previous combination.” This reduces repeated descriptions of instruments and measures. Readers can focus on shared rhythms, musical responses and how the ensemble changes their melody. The full scenario is to read my part, explore other instruments, compare combinations and return to my reading position.

name: source
text: Practice reference: Amber Sound Touch, “Memorising music”

**The first priorities are return, silence and entry feedback, and part comparison.** Later, a practice loop can lock the selection while the reader picks up an instrument, then alternate a model with a user-set practice interval, count-in and Stop. Amber Sound Touch describes short demonstrations and repeated playing. Voice annotations can preserve teacher advice by piece, part and measure, with reader-chosen review timing. Setup feedback can explain tracking status and give recovery cues or accept a spoken measure. **Current location and last valid location need distinct feedback.** I will also measure tracking accuracy and response time and log recovery.

I want both methods to have equivalent tasks, enough practice and comparable feedback. Second, which nonvisual information should I finish before reader testing? The selected measure, available instrument parts and a warning about silence are all possible priorities.
